chunks: What kind of load is a SoC/CPU?. The question: What type of load (resistive, inductive, capacitive) can a SoC/CPU typically be characterized as?
A SoC or CPU is made of millions of tiny CMOS switches. Each switch charges and discharges a small capacitor every clock tick.
So the best description of the chip as a load is a current sink (something that draws current) whose demand changes quickly, controlled by what the software is doing.
It is mostly capacitive in nature, but you rarely model it as a plain capacitor.
Imagine a city's water supply. At night, demand is a trickle. When everyone's alarm goes off, thousands of taps open at once and demand jumps in seconds.
The pipes and the water tower have to cope with the jump. The chip is the city, and the board's power supply is the pipe.
The picture breaks down because the chip's demand can change in nanoseconds.
The load is the die: a workload-controlled current source in parallel with on-die capacitance. The resistance and inductance (orange) are the delivery path.
The die capacitance supplies the first few nanoseconds of any current step; the inductance and resistance determine how quickly the rest can arrive.
CMOS: the type of transistor logic used in nearly all chips. Load: whatever draws current from a supply.
Dynamic power: the power used charging and discharging those tiny capacitors. It grows with the voltage squared and with the clock frequency. Transient: a quick change in current.
Droop: the temporary dip in the supply voltage when current jumps.
A core runs at 0. 9 volts and draws 54 amps. That is 48. 6 watts, and by Ohm's law, 0. 9 over 54 about 17 milliohms, so the chip looks like a 17 milliohms resistor.
But then the code goes idle and the current drops to almost nothing while the voltage stays at 0. 9 volts. The "resistance" just jumped, so it was never a real resistor.
"A SoC is best described as a capacitive, time-varying current sink. It's CMOS, so power goes into charging and discharging capacitance every cycle: alpha C V squared f .
On average it looks resistive, like 17 milliohms for a 54 amp core, but that's just V over I, and it changes with the workload. It isn't really inductive.
The inductance is in the package and board, and with fast current steps it causes droop, which is why the supply needs low impedance and lots of decoupling."
